clue.text: Obscure European coin

blocks.note: to obscure a light is to dim it
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A collector describes an unfamiliar coin from somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure European' reads as an adjective and noun describing the coin, but it is a verb plus an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dime is the American ten-cent piece, a familiar example of a coin.

clue.text: Leave suddenly, as banks of Danube affected

indicators.note: a river's banks are its two edges, so only the outside letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of the river's name
camp means exaggerated or affected in manner

explanation.surface: People abandon a place in a hurry because the Danube's banks are flooded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' looks like it means damaged by flooding, but it is the adjective meaning theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to depart abruptly or secretly, so it means to leave suddenly.

clue.text: Motorcycle was blue

blocks.note: first meaning: a light motorbike with pedals
second meaning: felt gloomy, past tense of a verb for being listless

explanation.surface: A motorbike was painted blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A moped is a small powered two-wheeler, and to have moped is to have sulked in low spirits.

clue.text: Really neat at university

blocks.note: a neat drink, with nothing added, is served straight
a student in residence at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: Someone insists a fellow student was truly tidy during their time at college.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge means being in residence there, a British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: As a slang exclamation or adverb, 'straight up' means honestly or truly, the same sense as really.

clue.text: To our sailors, trouble is a whirlwind

blocks.note: taken as written
the Royal Navy, Britain's own sailors
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Sailors reckon that a storm at sea means trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our sailors' means the British navy, from the setter's British standpoint.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air, a destructive type of whirlwind.

clue.text: One failing to gain a place in a lyceum, at first so put out

definitions.text: One failing to gain a place

indicators.note: at first means take only what comes at the start of each word

blocks.note: first letters of the two words
taken as written
a newspaper that put out a story ran it

explanation.surface: A student who failed to get into a school was upset at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like 'annoyed', but it is the verb for publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse or competitor that finishes outside the placings, hence an unsuccessful contender.

clue.text: Visit Chequers and call an election?

blocks.note: first meaning, literal: travel out to the Prime Minister's country house
second meaning: the idiom for a government seeking a fresh vote from the people

explanation.walkthrough: Chequers is the British Prime Minister's official country residence in Buckinghamshire, so a trip there is literally a trip into the rural countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: In British politics a leader who calls a general election is said to appeal to the nation, the idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Femme fatale, very French, dividing some office workers

indicators.note: something dividing a group splits it by sitting in the middle

blocks.note: temps are temporary office staff
très is French for very

explanation.surface: A seductive Frenchwoman causes rifts among the office staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A femme fatale is an alluring woman who leads men astray, which is what a temptress is.

clue.text: Spoiled parties, a freeloader

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and knocked out of shape, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Parties were ruined by a gatecrasher who came for the free food and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasite, figuratively, is a person who lives off others without contributing, just like a freeloader.

clue.text: Exercise equipment in flat brought by locals

blocks.note: flat means level, lying horizontal
a local is a neighbourhood pub, and pubs are bars; 'brought by' attaches them

explanation.surface: Neighbours carry gym equipment into somebody's apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is one's neighbourhood pub; 'flat' looks like an apartment but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Horizontal bars are the raised rods used in gymnastics, so they are gym apparatus.

clue.text: Committee's added to trophy cabinets

blocks.note: a cup is a typical sporting trophy
a board is a governing committee; with the 's it becomes the plural form

explanation.surface: A sports club committee has been put in charge of the trophy cabinets.
explanation.walkthrough: The committee comes first in the clue but is added after the trophy, since 'added to' places it on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupboards and cabinets are both pieces of furniture with shelves and doors for storage.

clue.text: Sailor carrying a maiden over a Devon river

indicators.note: in a down-reading sense 'over' turns the following letters back to front
something carrying another thing holds it inside itself

blocks.note: tar is an old slang word for a sailor
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for maiden, as in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A sailor ferries a young woman across a river in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden over' is a cricket term, an over with no runs scored, which disguises the turnaround of the two letters before they go inside the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tamar is the river forming most of the border between Devon and Cornwall in south-west England.

clue.text: Dessert wine produced by one artist

blocks.note: something produced has been made
the Roman numeral for one
RA stands for Royal Academician, a recognised artist

explanation.surface: A sweet wine turned out by a single painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese island of that name, often drunk with dessert.

clue.text: New toaster revolves

indicators.note: something new is a fresh version, so these letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A newly bought kitchen toaster turns round as it works.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn about an axis, which is what something that revolves does.

clue.text: I, for one, stick in a formal statement

blocks.note: the word I is an example of a pronoun
to cement is to stick things together

explanation.surface: Someone vows to stand firm on what they said officially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I, for one' looks like someone speaking for themselves; it is the word I as an example of a part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A pronouncement is an official declaration, a statement made formally and with authority.

clue.text: Salaciousness demonstrated in epic rerun, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests a different, possible version, so the letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Smutty content may be shown in the repeat of a lavish television drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Prurience is an excessive interest in sexual matters, the lewdness that salaciousness also describes.

clue.text: Puzzle brings on a vexed moment, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the phrase is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a vexed person is cross, and a tick is a moment

explanation.surface: A tricky puzzle causes a moment of irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A tick' is British slang for a short moment, as in 'just a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a word puzzle in which initial letters of lines spell out a word or message.

clue.text: Singers in bar turn on rest

indicators.note: to turn things over is to change their arrangement, so the next words are reordered

blocks.note: the counter in a pub is the bar
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Performers in a pub switch on the rest of the equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn on' reads as a phrasal verb, but only 'turn' is the signal; 'on' joins 'rest' as letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Countertenors are male vocalists who sing in the alto range, so they are a kind of singer.

clue.text: Composer and explorer, trendy one

blocks.note: Sir James Clark Ross, the polar explorer
something trendy is in
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A musician and a fashionable adventurer team up.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini was the Italian who wrote the operas The Barber of Seville and William Tell.

clue.text: Adaptable English remain in charge

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
to last is to remain or endure
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A flexible Englishman stays on as the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic, used figuratively, means flexible and able to adjust to circumstances, as adaptable does.

clue.text: One appearing in A Midsummer Night's Dream in a horse and trap

definitions.text: One appearing in A Midsummer Night's Dream

blocks.note: a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse
a spider's web is a trap for flies

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean actor arrives in a pony and trap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse and trap' reads as a carriage, but they are two separate pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobweb is one of Titania's fairy attendants in Shakespeare's comedy, so he is a character in that play.

clue.text: Birds, very big around Loire, surprisingly

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is not what was expected, so the river's letters land out of order
one part goes around the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very big sizes
taken as written

explanation.surface: Huge flocks of birds unexpectedly gather around France's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: Orioles are brightly coloured songbirds, so the plural answer names a group of birds.

clue.text: Food colourant - tons imported by an international organisation

indicators.note: goods imported by a country are brought inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: A global body brings in large quantities of food dye.
explanation.definitionFit: Annatto is an orange-red dye from achiote seeds, used to colour cheese and other foods.

clue.text: Food, piece of turkey, ready to eat

indicators.note: only a small piece is taken, here a single letter from the front

blocks.note: first letter of the word
fruit that is ready to eat is ripe

explanation.surface: Some turkey meat is cooked and ready to be served.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe, the stomach lining of cattle, is eaten as food, especially in northern England.

clue.text: Loose flowing garment worn by head of northern island group

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
something worn by a person is wrapped around them, so one part encloses the other

blocks.note: the loose robe worn in ancient Rome
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A loose robe worn by a chief from the north of an archipelago.
explanation.walkthrough: The garment goes around the single letter, as clothes go around a body.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom made up of over a hundred islands in the South Pacific.

clue.text: Question and answer session in Bury to contend with

blocks.note: to inter is to bury
to vie is to compete or contend
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Something awkward to put up with during a questioning in the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury looks like the name of the English town, capitalised at the start of the wordplay, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An interview is a meeting in which one person asks questions and another replies, as for a job or the press.

clue.text: Conservative speeches I prepared for a bishop, for example

indicators.note: something prepared has been worked up and arranged, so these letters are reorganised

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Tory politician has written addresses for a senior churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The bishop looks like a clergyman in a political story; he is the piece that moves diagonally on a board.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is one of the pieces in the game of chess, so it is an example of the answer.

clue.text: Rosemary, say, in Father Brown

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A woman named Rosemary appears in a Father Brown detective story.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary looks like a woman's name, perhaps a character in G. K. Chesterton's Father Brown stories, but it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is an aromatic plant used in cooking, an example of a herb.
